lead: Software configuration management (SCM) is the set of practices that keeps every work product under control. A work product can be code, a requirements document, a test case, a build script or a database schema. SCM gives each such item a name and a version, stores it, and allows a change only through an approved route. It exists because many people edit shared products and because a released product must be rebuilt exactly. You meet SCM in every version control system, every change request, and every CI/CD pipeline that builds from a tagged commit.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the project plan, and Unit 5 for version control and CI/CD basics.

blocks.text: A configuration item (CI) is any work product that SCM treats as a unit. Typical CIs are a source file, a requirements section, a test plan, a build script and a release note. Each CI has an identifier, a version and an owner. A version is one saved state of the CI; version 1.2 is not better than 1.1, it is a later state.

A baseline is an approved, frozen set of CI versions. It is the reference for later work. If baseline B1 holds login 1.0, SRS 1.0 and test plan 1.0, a developer may change a private copy, but the baseline stays fixed. A change enters the baseline only after approval. Write it as B1 = {login 1.0, SRS 1.0, test plan 1.0}. The braces list the CIs and versions; the numbers after each name are versions.

Baselines stop uncontrolled drift. A tester can report a defect against B1 and know exactly which code and documents were tested. A build can be repeated from B1 years later. Without a baseline, the latest version changes every hour and nobody can say what was tested or released.

sections.h3: Change control, status accounting and audit

blocks.text: A change request (CR) is a written request to change a baseline. It states the CI, the reason, the proposed new version and any linked defects. Impact analysis estimates affected CIs, effort and risk before a decision. The change control board (CCB) is a small group that approves or rejects the CR. The CCB does not usually write the code; it guards the baseline.

items: Record CR-07 with the requested change and its reason.
Analyse impact: which CIs, test cases and releases are affected.
Send the CR to the CCB for approve or reject.
If approved, make the change in a branch, review and test it.
Update the affected CIs and write a new baseline.
Tell affected teams and record the decision.

blocks.text: Status accounting is the record of each CI and CR through its life: open, under review, approved, implemented, released or rejected. It answers what happened to CR-07. Configuration audit checks reality against records. A functional audit asks whether the delivered item meets requirements; a physical audit asks whether the correct versions, documents and build inputs are present. Audit catches a release that was built from an unrecorded local change.

sections.h3: Version control, build records and CI/CD

blocks.text: Version control stores each CI and its history. It supports branches for parallel work and tags for baselines. A tag such as B2 is a fixed name for a set of versions. The repository alone is not SCM; it is the storage layer for SCM records. See Unit 5, Version control systems.

A build record lists the source versions, compiler or tool versions, dependencies and commands used for one build. A release record lists the CIs delivered to users, the approved CRs, test evidence and the rollback version. These records make a build reproducible and an audit possible.

In CI/CD, each pipeline run should start from a recorded commit or tag and write its result to an artifact repository. A pipeline that builds from a developer's uncommitted folder breaks SCM. A pipeline that tags every release and stores the build record makes SCM automatic. The pipeline does not replace the CCB; it enforces the approved baseline and records what it built. See 6.9 for the release package and rollback plan.

figure.caption: Baseline B1 and the new baseline B2 after CR-07: login goes 1.0 → 1.1 and the test plan goes 1.0 → 1.1, while SRS stays at 1.0. Two of the three items changed, so B2 is the new frozen baseline.

spec.title: B1 and B2 after CR-07
spec.aria: Two rows: baseline B1 holds login 1.0, SRS 1.0 and test plan 1.0; baseline B2 after CR-07 holds login 1.1, SRS 1.0 and test plan 1.1, with login and test plan marked as the two changed items.

examples.question: Baseline B1 has login module 1.0, SRS 1.0 and test plan 1.0. CR-07 is approved and changes login to 1.1 and test plan to 1.1. Write baseline B2 and say how many items changed.
steps: List B1: login = 1.0, SRS = 1.0, test plan = 1.0.
Apply the approved CR to login: login changes from 1.0 to 1.1.
Apply the approved CR to the test plan: test plan changes from 1.0 to 1.1.
SRS is not in the CR, so SRS stays at 1.0.
Write B2: login = 1.1, SRS = 1.0, test plan = 1.1.
Compare B1 and B2: login changed and test plan changed. Count = 2 items.
examples.answer: B2 has login 1.1, SRS 1.0 and test plan 1.1; 2 items changed.
examples.check:
b1 = {'login': '1.0', 'srs': '1.0', 'test_plan': '1.0'}
b2 = dict(b1)
b2['login'] = '1.1'
b2['test_plan'] = '1.1'
changed = sum(1 for k in b1 if b1[k] != b2[k])
print(changed)

traps: Treating version control as the whole of SCM. SCM also covers change control, status accounting and audits.
Calling the latest version a baseline. A baseline is an approved frozen set, not whatever was saved last.
Letting the CCB skip impact analysis. The board needs affected CIs, effort and risk before it approves or rejects.
Confusing status accounting with configuration audit. Status accounting reports history; audit checks that records match the real product.
Ignoring build and release records. Without them a release cannot be rebuilt or audited.

quiz.a: A configuration item is a work product treated as a unit by SCM, with an identifier and version. A baseline is an approved, frozen set of CI versions used as a reference.

quiz.q: What is the role of the change control board?
quiz.a: The CCB approves or rejects change requests after impact analysis. It guards the baseline and does not usually write the code.

quiz.q: Why is a version control repository not the whole of SCM?
quiz.a: The repository stores versions and history. SCM also needs change control through CRs and the CCB, status accounting for each item and CR, configuration audits, and build and release records.

quiz.q: Baseline B3 has A 2.0, B 3.1 and C 1.4. CR-11 changes B to 3.2 and C to 1.5. Write B4 and count the changed items.
quiz.a: B4 has A 2.0, B 3.2 and C 1.5. B and C changed, so the count is 2 items.

quiz.q: A build record must list four kinds of input. Name them.
quiz.a: Source versions, tool or compiler versions, dependencies, and build commands.

quiz.q: A release was built from a local uncommitted change. Which SCM activity should catch this, and how?
quiz.a: Configuration audit should catch it. A physical audit compares the release and build record with the repository baseline and finds that the built source version is not the approved version.

quiz.q: The CCB rejects CR-07. What happens to the baseline and to the status record?
quiz.a: The baseline does not change. The status record marks CR-07 as rejected, with the reason and date, so the decision can be traced later.

quiz.q: State the difference between status accounting and configuration audit.
quiz.a: Status accounting records the life history of each CI and CR. Configuration audit checks that the delivered product and its records match the approved baseline and requirements.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern SCM is moving toward GitOps, where the approved repository state is applied automatically to production. Supply-chain security adds signed build provenance, so a release record can prove which source and tools produced an artifact. Artifact repositories and policy engines now enforce baseline rules inside CI/CD. Useful search terms are software configuration management plan, configuration audit, build provenance and SLSA.
